in_text_mentions: ies were further processed, producing additional serial sections that were subjected to D2-40 immunohistochemistry to facilitate detection of lymphatic vessels. This resulted in identification of multiple foci of widely dilated lymphatic vessels that were predominantly localized in subpleural and peribronchial areas and greatly obscured by secondary changes, including thickened pleura and evidence of organizing broncho-pneumonia (Figure 3). These findings are characteristic of DPL, but had been difficult to detect because of the focal pattern of presentation and secondary inflammatory changes.

panels.attribution_text: Zhang et al. Case Report: Diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis in a child.. Frontiers in pediatrics 2025. doi:10.3389/fped.2025.1591611. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (A,B) Presents post-operative histopathological staining of microscopically distorted lymphatic ducts.
in_text_mentions: Postoperative histological examination confirmed lymphangiomatosis involving the mediastinum, right lower lobe of the lung, and pericardium, characterized by numerous tortuous and dilated lymphatic vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated the following profile: CD31 (+), D2-40 (+), TIF-1 (+), CKp (−), CD34 (+), SMA (+), Ki-67 ≈ 3% (Figure 3), NTRK (−), and S100 (−). Integrating the clinical presentation, imaging findings, and pathological results, a final diagnosis of GLA was established.

A: Panel A chest CT from DPL case report shows massive right pleural effusion, a classic DPL manifestation; disease attribution supported by DPL-focused article title plus panel-specific effusion. B: Panel B chest CT shows thickening of the lobular septum, directly matching smooth interlobular septal thickening vocabulary in known DPL case. A total of 9 pericardial pathologies were reviewed at Liuzhou People's Hospital (Fig. 2A and B), revealing a vascular tumor that included lymphangioma and hemangioma. Lymphangioma accounted for 50% to 80% of each section, and the morphology mainly reflected cavernous lymphangioma. However, DPL is rare, and we lacked related treatment experience. He was treated with systemic oral corticosteroids (30 mg/day for 2 months). panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Chest CT panel in DPL case report with caption explicit diffuse interlobular septal thickening, matching vocabulary finding. B: CT mediastinal window showing mediastinal enlargement without enhancement and pleural effusion in confirmed DPL adult case. C: Real patient bronchoscopy showing edematous changes and diffuse thin-walled translucent vesicles of DPL, but no matching finding_key in allowed vocabulary, so excluded per findings rule. D: NBI bronchoscopy companion to C showing same diffuse vesicles/edema, no vocabulary finding_key covers bronchoscopy lesions, so excluded. E: HE lung histology showing proliferative irregular lymphatic vessels in DPL case, matching anastomosing lymphatic channels finding. F: D2-40 IHC revealing proliferative lymphatic channels, diagnostic of DPL lymphatic proliferation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real patient pulmonary CT showing extensive pleural effusion and pericardial effusion, classic manifestations of diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis in a child. Pleural effusion maps to the chylous pleural effusion finding; pericardial effusion is not in the vocabulary and is proposed. B: Real patient pulmonary CT showing interstitial thickening, corresponding to interlobular septal thickening, a recognized CT manifestation of diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis. C: Real patient pulmonary CT showing diffuse ground-glass opacities, a recognized but vocabulary-absent manifestation of diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis. The finding is clearly present and captioned, so the panel is included with the finding proposed.
panels.attribution_text: Zhang et al. Case Report: Diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis in a child.. Frontiers in pediatrics 2025. doi:10.3389/fped.2025.1591611. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Demonstrates extensive pleural effusion and pericardial effusion on the patient's pulmonary CT scan; (B) reveals interstitial thickening; and (C) shows diffuse ground-glass opacities within the lungs.
in_text_mentions: Postoperative histological examination confirmed lymphangiomatosis involving the mediastinum, right lower lobe of the lung, and pericardium, characterized by numerous tortuous and dilated lymphatic vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated the following profile: CD31 (+), D2-40 (+), TIF-1 (+), CKp (−), CD34 (+), SMA (+), Ki-67 ≈ 3% (Figure 3), NTRK (−), and S100 (−). Integrating the clinical presentation, imaging findings, and pathological results, a final diagnosis of GLA was established.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: CD31 immunohistochemistry panel from the diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis case report; brown membranous staining highlights anastomosing lymphatic channels in lung tissue, supporting the diagnosis. The supplied caption describes a chest CT, but the rendered figure is IHC; classification follows the visible image together with the disease-focused article title. B: SAM immunostain panel of the same DPL lung biopsy, part of the histologic demonstration of the lymphatic-channel lesion. Caption/image mismatch noted; classified from the visible IHC and the article title. C: D2-40 (podoplanin) immunohistochemistry strongly labels lymphatic endothelium of the anastomosing channels, a classic histologic feature of diffuse pulmonary lymphangiomatosis. D: Ki-67 proliferation-marker panel of the DPL biopsy, completing the histologic demonstration of the lymphatic-channel lesion. Classified from the visible IHC despite the CT-oriented caption.

in_text_mentions: ffusion accompanied by pericardial membrane thickening (2). Affected tissues generally appear hypodense, demonstrating water-like attenuation patterns on imaging. Enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes are commonly observed, often accompanied by pleural thickening or effusion. In addition, enlarged hypodense cervical and/or axillary lymph nodes with indistinct margins and minimal enhancement on contrast-enhanced imaging are frequently reported (3). The radiologic findings in the present case are illustrated in Figure 4. Collectively, these imaging features provide important diagnostic clues for GLA.
